newsitem.title: CHINA: China police swoop on letter-writing dissident.
newsitem.headline: China police swoop on letter-writing dissident.

text.p: Chinese police on Monday detained veteran dissident Jin Cheng for the second time since he issued a daring call last week for public justice in the case of a disgraced Beijing leader, the activist's wife said.

Jin remained in custody more than 10 hours after he was seized by three plainclothes police officers outside his western Beijing home at 7.30 a.m. (2330 GMT Sunday), the former official's wife, Liu Xiuli, said by telephone.
"I telephoned them a little while ago and they said they were still not letting him go, but they gave no reason," Liu said. "Of course, I am very worried."

Jin last week sent an open letter to the head of China's National People's Congress, or parliament, calling for former Beijing Communist Party chief Chen Xitong to be punished for prompting a bloody crackdown on pro-democracy protests in 1989.
Two days after Jin posted the letter, Beijing police detained the 38-year-old activist overnight.
Appeals and petitions to the communist-led government that touch on sensitive issues are a risky political act in China, which has clamped down hard on dissent in recent years.

Other dissidents in the Chinese capital said on Monday they had been warned to keep out of circulation for several days during a visit by U.S. National Security Adviser Sandy Berger, who arrived on Sunday and was due to leave on Wednesday.
Prominent activist Ren Wanding accused police of putting a 24-hour guard around his home and banning him from going outside.

Ren, a veteran pro-democracy campaigner who spent seven years in prison after the army crushed student-led protests centred on Beijing's Tiananmen Square in 1989, said he was furious at the limits on his freedom.
Activist Jin, who was jailed for publishing an underground magazine after the 1989 crackdown, said last week he was not afraid of the consequences of his appeal for public justice.

Jin has been the target of police surveillance and occasional detention since his release in 1993 and has scraped out a living as a freelance artist since being dismissed from his job as an official at Beijing's International Conference Centre.
